e.title: $e$ has EML complexity at most 1
e.natural_language_statement: The constant $e$ is the value of a valid closed EML tree with one node: $\mathrm{eml}(1,1) = e^1 - \ln 1 = e$.
e.source: Odrzywolek, All elementary functions from a single operator, arXiv:2603.21852 (2026), Section 4.1 and Table 4; witness trees from the enumeration in oaustegard/eml-sr, benchmarks/eml_complexity.md (2026-09-04)
e.formal_statement:
namespace EmlComplexity
theorem attains_e : Attains (Real.exp 1) 1 := by sorry
end EmlComplexity

e-1.title: $e-1$ has EML complexity at most 2
e-1.natural_language_statement: The constant $e - 1$ is the value of a valid closed EML tree with two nodes: $\mathrm{eml}(1, \mathrm{eml}(1,1)) = e - \ln e = e - 1$.
e-1.source: Odrzywolek, All elementary functions from a single operator, arXiv:2603.21852 (2026), Section 4.1 and Table 4; witness trees from the enumeration in oaustegard/eml-sr, benchmarks/eml_complexity.md (2026-09-04)
e-1.formal_statement:
namespace EmlComplexity
theorem attains_e_sub_one : Attains (Real.exp 1 - 1) 2 := by sorry
end EmlComplexity

0.title: $0$ has EML complexity at most 3
0.natural_language_statement: The constant $0$ is the value of a valid closed EML tree with three nodes: $\mathrm{eml}(1, \mathrm{eml}(\mathrm{eml}(1,1),1)) = e - \ln(e^{e}) = 0$. Three is the least size at which a real closed tree evaluates to $0$ (that minimality is not part of this statement).
0.source: Odrzywolek, All elementary functions from a single operator, arXiv:2603.21852 (2026), Section 4.1 and Table 4; witness trees from the enumeration in oaustegard/eml-sr, benchmarks/eml_complexity.md (2026-09-04)
0.formal_statement:
namespace EmlComplexity
theorem attains_zero : Attains ((0 : ℝ)) 3 := by sorry
end EmlComplexity

e-2.title: $e-2$ has EML complexity at most 7
e-2.natural_language_statement: The constant $e - 2$ is the value of a valid closed EML tree with seven nodes. The tree computes $\ln(e-1)$ in five nodes and then subtracts $1$ through $\exp(\ln(e-1)) - \ln e$.
e-2.source: Odrzywolek, All elementary functions from a single operator, arXiv:2603.21852 (2026), Section 4.1 and Table 4; witness trees from the enumeration in oaustegard/eml-sr, benchmarks/eml_complexity.md (2026-09-04)
e-2.formal_statement:
namespace EmlComplexity
theorem attains_e_sub_two : Attains (Real.exp 1 - 2) 7 := by sorry
end EmlComplexity

-1.title: $-1$ has EML complexity at most 8
-1.natural_language_statement: The constant $-1$ is the value of a valid closed EML tree with eight nodes: $\exp(\ln(e-1)) - \ln(e^{e}) = (e - 1) - e$.
-1.source: Odrzywolek, All elementary functions from a single operator, arXiv:2603.21852 (2026), Section 4.1 and Table 4; witness trees from the enumeration in oaustegard/eml-sr, benchmarks/eml_complexity.md (2026-09-04)
-1.formal_statement:
namespace EmlComplexity
theorem attains_neg_one : Attains ((-1 : ℝ)) 8 := by sorry
end EmlComplexity

2.title: $2$ has EML complexity at most 9
2.natural_language_statement: The integer $2$ is the value of a valid closed EML tree with nine nodes: $e - \ln\big(\exp(\ln(e-1) - 1)\big) = e - (e - 2) = 2$.
2.source: Odrzywolek, All elementary functions from a single operator, arXiv:2603.21852 (2026), Section 4.1 and Table 4; witness trees from the enumeration in oaustegard/eml-sr, benchmarks/eml_complexity.md (2026-09-04)
2.formal_statement:
namespace EmlComplexity
theorem attains_two : Attains ((2 : ℝ)) 9 := by sorry
end EmlComplexity

ln2.title: $\ln 2$ has EML complexity at most 12
ln2.natural_language_statement: The constant $\ln 2$ is the value of a valid closed EML tree with twelve nodes: the nine-node tree for $2$ wrapped in the three-node logarithm $\ln x = \mathrm{eml}(1, \mathrm{eml}(\mathrm{eml}(1, x), 1))$.
ln2.source: Odrzywolek, All elementary functions from a single operator, arXiv:2603.21852 (2026), Section 4.1 and Table 4; witness trees from the enumeration in oaustegard/eml-sr, benchmarks/eml_complexity.md (2026-09-04)
ln2.formal_statement:
namespace EmlComplexity
theorem attains_log_two : Attains (Real.log 2) 12 := by sorry
end EmlComplexity

3.title: $3$ has EML complexity at most 14
3.natural_language_statement: The integer $3$ is the value of a valid closed EML tree with fourteen nodes, built as $e - (e - 3)$ from the twelve-node tree for $e - 3 = \ln(\exp(e-2)) - 1$ in the same subtraction pattern as $2$.
3.source: Odrzywolek, All elementary functions from a single operator, arXiv:2603.21852 (2026), Section 4.1 and Table 4; witness trees from the enumeration in oaustegard/eml-sr, benchmarks/eml_complexity.md (2026-09-04)
3.formal_statement:
namespace EmlComplexity
theorem attains_three : Attains ((3 : ℝ)) 14 := by sorry
end EmlComplexity

1/2.title: $1/2$ has EML complexity at most 17
1/2.natural_language_statement: The constant $1/2$ is the value of a valid closed EML tree with seventeen nodes: $\exp(-\ln 2)$, where $\ln 2$ is built as $e - \ln(\exp(e - \ln 2))$ from the nine-node tree for $2$.
1/2.source: Odrzywolek, All elementary functions from a single operator, arXiv:2603.21852 (2026), Section 4.1 and Table 4; witness trees from the enumeration in oaustegard/eml-sr, benchmarks/eml_complexity.md (2026-09-04)
1/2.formal_statement:
namespace EmlComplexity
theorem attains_half : Attains ((1 / 2 : ℝ)) 17 := by sorry
end EmlComplexity

-3.title: $-3$ has EML complexity at most 20
-3.natural_language_statement: The integer $-3$ is the value of a valid closed EML tree with twenty nodes: $\exp(\ln(e^{e} - 3)) - \ln(\exp(e^{e}))$, where $e^{e} - 3$ is reached by three subtractions of $1$ from $e^{e}$.
-3.source: Odrzywolek, All elementary functions from a single operator, arXiv:2603.21852 (2026), Section 4.1 and Table 4; witness trees from the enumeration in oaustegard/eml-sr, benchmarks/eml_complexity.md (2026-09-04)
-3.formal_statement:
namespace EmlComplexity
theorem attains_neg_three : Attains ((-3 : ℝ)) 20 := by sorry
end EmlComplexity

4.title: $4$ has EML complexity at most 21
4.natural_language_statement: The integer $4$ is the value of a valid closed EML tree with twenty-one nodes: $e^{e} - \ln\big(\exp(e^{e} - 4)\big)$, where $e^{e} - 4$ is reached by four subtractions of $1$ from $e^{e}$. Real-branch enumeration to size 20 finds no smaller tree; that lower bound is a separate open statement.
4.source: Odrzywolek, All elementary functions from a single operator, arXiv:2603.21852 (2026), Section 4.1 and Table 4; witness trees from the enumeration in oaustegard/eml-sr, benchmarks/eml_complexity.md (2026-09-04)
4.formal_statement:
namespace EmlComplexity
theorem attains_four : Attains ((4 : ℝ)) 21 := by sorry
end EmlComplexity
